items.title: Trump administration sues to block certification of upcoming Alaska election
items.summary: The Trump administration has filed a federal lawsuit seeking to block the certification of Alaska's Senate election results if Republican Senator Dan Sullivan loses to Democrat Mary Peltola. The government argues that the presence of another candidate named Dan Sullivan on the ballot could confuse voters and distort the election's integrity.

brief.what: The US Justice Department is suing to prevent Alaska from certifying its Senate election results if the incumbent Republican, Dan Sullivan, loses by a margin smaller than the votes received by a second candidate also named Dan Sullivan. The administration contends that the ballot inclusion of the second candidate, a retired teacher, creates voter confusion that threatens the integrity of the electoral process.
brief.who: The main actors include US President Donald Trump, who supports the legal challenge; Republican Senator Dan Sullivan; Democratic challenger Mary Peltola; and the second candidate, Dan J Sullivan, who denies his candidacy is a political maneuver.
brief.context: This legal action follows previous unsuccessful attempts to remove the second Dan Sullivan from the ballot, which were rejected by the Alaska Supreme Court. Alaska utilizes a ranked-choice voting system, which allows voters to select multiple candidates.
brief.why: The Justice Department claims the second candidate's presence is a 'scam' intended to siphon votes from the incumbent to benefit Peltola's campaign, thereby distorting the will of Alaskan voters.
brief.next: The lawsuit requests that certification be delayed pending an investigation if the election outcome is close enough to suggest voter confusion occurred.

brief.next: Boohoo plans to transition its Burnley warehouse into a new fulfilment hub operated by GXO, with net debt expected to be negligible by the end of the year.

items.title: Kennedy to select MAHA-aligned researcher to head mental health institute, overruling NIH director
items.author: Jocelyn Kaiser
items.summary: The U.S. health secretary intends to appoint a proponent of metabolic psychiatry to lead the National Institute of Mental Health. This decision reportedly bypasses the authority of the NIH director.

brief.what: The health secretary plans to appoint a leader aligned with the MAHA movement to head the $2.2 billion National Institute of Mental Health. This appointment will occur despite opposition from the NIH director.
brief.who: The health secretary, the NIH director, and an unnamed researcher associated with the metabolic psychiatry movement.
brief.context: The National Institute of Mental Health is a major federal agency responsible for mental health research, currently operating with a $2.2 billion budget.
brief.why: The health secretary is overruling the NIH director to install a researcher who supports the metabolic psychiatry movement.

items.title: First person infected with rare Shamonda virus: what we know
items.author: Rachel Fieldhouse
items.summary: A man in France has become the first recorded human case of the Shamonda virus following an ongoing outbreak in European livestock. Researchers are investigating the transmission routes of this orthobunyavirus, which currently lacks specific vaccines or antiviral treatments.

brief.what: A man in France with leukemia has died after contracting the Shamonda virus, marking the first known human infection. The virus, which has been circulating in European cattle since July, caused severe neurological symptoms including seizures and a coma.
brief.who: The patient, an immunocompromised man in France, and infectious-disease researchers including Krispin Hajkowicz and Daniel Rawle.
brief.context: Shamonda virus is an orthobunyavirus typically found in livestock and transmitted by midges. While human-to-human transmission has not been recorded for this specific virus, experts note that climate change and increased human-wildlife contact are raising the risk of zoonotic infections.
brief.why: Researchers suggest the man was likely infected via a midge bite, though they are investigating other potential routes like contaminated food or medical procedures. Experts attribute the rising risk of such infections to climate change, increased contact with livestock, and a growing population of immunocompromised individuals.
brief.next: Investigations are ongoing to rule out alternative transmission routes such as contaminated food or blood transfusions.

items.title: Elusive snow leopards and evasive particles: Books in brief
items.author: Andrew Robinson
items.summary: A review of recent books explores the evolution of quantum physics, the history of US pharmaceutical research, and the cultural foundations of algorithmic communication.

brief.what: Nature reviews three new books covering diverse scientific and technical subjects, including the quantum world, the history of US pharmaceutical research, and the development of algorithmic culture. The works examine topics ranging from the physics of black holes to the long-term investment strategies that have sustained American drug research for an eighty-year-long period.
brief.who: Physicist Danni Holmes, journalist Barry Werth, and communication researcher Xiaochang Li are the authors of the books reviewed.
brief.context: The reviews highlight how scientific progress is often intertwined with historical, financial, and cultural developments, such as the influence of presidential science advisers on pharmacology and the linguistic debates shaping modern artificial intelligence.
brief.why: The books were written to provide analysis on complex topics, with Werth specifically aiming to illuminate the value of long-term investment in science through the lens of post-war pharmacology leaders.
